Why SARSA walks the long way on CliffWalking

text: Week 4: Q-learning and tabular control. Control means learning action values , so that acting greedily needs no model: pi(s) = argmax a Q(s,a) . SARSA (on-policy) Q-learning (off-policy) Update target R t+1 + gamma Q(S t+1 , A t+1 ) R t+1 + gamma max a' Q(S t+1 , a') Learns the value of the epsilon -greedy policy it follows the greedy (optimal) policy Converges to q pi of the behaviour policy (→ q as epsilon → 0) q , under standard step-size conditions Both converge under the Robbins–Monro conditions sum t alpha t = infty and sum t alpha t 2 < infty , provided every state-action pair keeps being visited. Code: rl/tabular.py , with linearly decaying epsilon and random tie-breaking in argmax . Results (3 seeds, greedy evaluation; scripts/run tabular.py ). Environment Value iteration (optimal) Q-learning SARSA FrozenLake 4×4, slippery: success rate 0.729 0.734 ± 0.004 0.727 ± 0.001 Taxi: return 7.91 7.91 ± 0.00 7.72 ± 0.09 CliffWalking: return −13 −13 ± 0 −17 ± 0 Why SARSA walks the long way on CliffWalking. Stepping off the cliff costs −100. Q-learning's target uses the max over next actions, so it ignores the chance that exploration pushes it off the edge. It learns the optimal edge path (13 steps, −13). SARSA's target uses the action actually taken, including epsilon -random ones, so cells next to the cliff look dangerous and it learns a safer path one row up (−17). Neither is "wrong": SARSA optimises the policy it actually runs, Q-learning the one it would run without exploration. Limitations that motivate DQN. A Q-table needs one entry per (state, action). Taxi has 500 states, but CartPole's state is four continuous numbers and Atari's is 84×84×4 pixels. We need function approximation , Q(s,a;theta) , which generalises across similar states.
